{{Short description|American theoretical physicist}}
'''Vernon Duane Barger''' (born June 5, 1938, in [[Curllsville, Pennsylvania]])<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is an American theoretical physicist, specializing in elementary particle physics.

==Education and career==
Barger graduated from [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 1960 with a B.S. in engineering science and in 1963 with a Ph.D. in theoretical physics. His doctoral advisor was Emil Kazes.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|name=Vernon Duane Barger|id=274741}}</ref> In the physics department of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] (UW–Madison), Barger became in 1963 a research associate, in 1965 an assistant professor, in 1968 full professor, and in 1983 the J. H. Van Vleck Professor of Physics. At UW–Madison he held a Hillsdale Professorship from 1987 to 1991 and since 1991 has held a Vilas Professorship.<ref>{{cite news|title=Barger Wins 2000 Hilldale Award|newspaper=The Wisconsin Physicist: A Newsletter for University of Wisconsin Physics Alumni, Winter 2000–2001|page=5|url=https://www.physics.wisc.edu/newsletter/news00.pdf}}</ref>

Barger has done research on [[collider]] physics phenomenology (especially related to the [[Large Hadron Collider]]), [[Higgs boson]]s, [[supersymmetry]], and the [[Grand Unified Theory]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Vernon Barger|url=https://www.physics.wisc.edu/directory/barger-vernon/|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison}}</ref> as well as "[[neutrino oscillations]], particle [[dark matter]], [[early universe cosmology]], heavy [[quark]]s and the [[Regge pole]] model."<ref name=SakuraiPrize>{{cite web|title=2021 J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics Recipient, Vernon Barger|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Barger&first_nm=Vernon&year=2021}}</ref>

He has held visiting appointments at [[CERN]] (1972), at [[Durham University]] (1983), at the [[University of Hawaii]] (1970, 1979, and 1982), at the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Santa Barbara, at [[Rutherford Appleton Laboratory]] (1972), at [[SLAC]] (1975), at the [[University of Tokyo]], and at the [[University of Washington]].<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>

Barger was elected in 1977 a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1977&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Wisconsin}} (search on year 1977 and institution University of Wisconsin)</ref> He was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] for the academic year 1971–1972.<ref>{{cite web|title=Vernon D. Barger|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/vernon-d-barger/|access-date=2022-04-11|archive-date=2022-04-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220411081559/https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/vernon-d-barger/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1998 he was a Frontier Fellow am [[Fermilab]]. In 2021 he received the [[Sakurai Prize]] for "pioneering work in collider physics contributing to the discovery and characterization of the [[W boson]], [[top quark]], and Higgs boson, and for the development of incisive strategies to test theoretical ideas with experiments."<ref name=SakuraiPrize/>
